screens.title: Auditing and Logging in Hyperledger Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: Logging and auditing form the backbone of operational visibility for an enterprise blockchain. In Fabric, peers, orderers, certificate authorities, and client applications each emit logs that, when collected correctly, let you trace transactions, verify identity operations, and investigate incidents. This lesson will help you recognize the essential audit trails Fabric produces, configure logging verbosity safely, and move logs into a centralized system so they are durable and searchable. For example, you will learn how to set an environment variable to raise verbosity for the gossip protocol without flooding the entire network, how chaincode prints appear in peer logs, and why shipping container output to a central store matters for compliance. We'll also highlight common mistakes operators make, such as leaving debug-level logs on in production or failing to correlate transaction IDs across components. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to configure, interpret, and centralize Fabric logs to support troubleshooting, alerting, and audits. Consider what one successful transaction trace might reveal about peer health in your environment.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Auditing and Logging
Auditing and Logging in Hyperledger Fabric
Observe transactions, configure verbosity, and centralize logs for reliable audits.
In this lesson
Understand Fabric log sources, learn FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC usage, diagnose transaction flows, and design centralized logging.
What you will do
Inspect container logs, change FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC, restart the test network, and observe chaincode output in peer logs.
Why this matters

Persistent, centralized logs let you answer who did what and why, satisfy auditors, and reduce mean-time-to-repair during incidents.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: In this first set of objectives we focus on foundational understanding and configuration skills. You will first learn why comprehensive logging and auditing are essential: logs provide the evidence trail needed for compliance, forensic analysis, and operational debugging. A concrete example is extracting a transaction lifecycle from peer and orderer logs to reconstruct a disputed state change. Second, you'll learn how to configure logging levels for Fabric components using environment variables. Practically, this means editing container environment settings or process variables so FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC drives global and module-specific verbosity. We will show how an operator can raise gossip module verbosity without increasing noise from unrelated modules. Each objective pairs a skill with why it matters in production: better diagnostics, minimal performance impact, and audit readiness. As you study, consider how you would handle a live incident where a single peer reports timeouts. Which logs would you raise temporarily and how would you preserve them for later analysis?

screens.title: Why comprehensive logging and auditing matter
screens.narratorSegment: Comprehensive logging and auditing mean you collect, preserve, and analyze records that prove what happened in your Fabric network and why. Logs are more than noise; they are the evidentiary trail auditors and incident responders use. For example, when a financial asset appears with an unexpected owner, transaction lifecycle logs from the peer and orderer can show when the proposal arrived, which endorsement results were returned, when ordering placed the transaction, and when peers committed the change. A common misconception is that local container logs are sufficient. In production they are not: container restarts can delete log buffers and distributed components produce scattered fragments that are hard to correlate. Good auditing requires centralized storage, timestamp consistency, and identifiable transaction IDs. Practically, you will map which log entries correspond to key steps: proposal reception, endorsement, ordering, and commit confirmations. One simple operational test is to deploy a chaincode with a print in its execution path and then perform an invoke; the chaincode print should appear in the peer's log with module tags that let you attach it to the transaction ID. Ask yourself: if a peer and an orderer disagree on state, which logs will you pull first and what identifiers will you use to link them together?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Why logging matters
Definition
Comprehensive logging and auditing collect detailed, timestamped events across components to support diagnosis and compliance.
Concrete example
Deploy a chaincode that prints a trace message. Invoke it and verify the chaincode print appears in the peer log with a transaction ID, then follow that ID through orderer and commit logs.
Common misconception
Assuming local docker logs are sufficient. In production, ephemeral containers and distributed components make centralized retention necessary.
Key Takeaway

Treat logs as audit records: persist them externally, ensure timestamps and IDs are usable, and use them first when reconstructing incidents.

Where audit value appears
  • Transaction lifecycle logs show proposal → endorsement → ordering → commit.
  • Chaincode prints reveal business logic behavior during execution.
  • MSP entries document identity validation and cert handling.
  • Gossip logs explain peer discovery and state synchronization issues.
Check your understanding
When an invoke fails intermittently, collect peer gossip, chaincode, and orderer logs and correlate by transaction ID to identify where the flow breaks.

screens.title: Using FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC to control verbosity
screens.narratorSegment: FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC is the primary control for Fabric logging. It is an environment variable that sets a global level and optionally raises or lowers verbosity for named modules. For example, using INFO:gossip=DEBUG keeps overall noise at informational level but produces detailed gossip messages to help with peer discovery or synchronization issues. A practical workflow is to add this environment variable to your peer or orderer container definition, restart the service, and observe the change. A common mistake is to set DEBUG globally in production, which can flood your logging pipeline and affect performance. Instead, target only the module you need. In the lab activity you will edit a docker-compose service block for a peer and an orderer to set FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC to DEBUG, restart the network, and then revert back after collecting the necessary output. When speaking about setting variables, remember that many Fabric components also expose logging settings in their YAML config files but the environment variable is the quickest way to change runtime verbosity. Using FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC to control verbosity means use fabric_logging_spec to adjust global and per-module logging levels at runtime.. In practical terms, set global and module-specific logging without rebuilding components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC control
keyIdea.text: Use FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC to adjust global and per-module logging levels at runtime.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC
Definition and usage
FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC accepts a global level and optional module overrides, for example INFO:gossip=DEBUG.
Add it to your docker-compose environment section or export it when launching a single container. This allows targeted troubleshooting without rebuilding binaries or changing YAML permanently.
Quick example
services:
  peer0.org1.example.com:
    environment:
      - FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC=INFO:gossip=DEBUG
      - CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED=true

  orderer.example.com:
    environment:
      - FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC=DEBUG
      - ORDERER_GENERAL_TLS_ENABLED=true
Add these lines under each service's environment section, then restart the network to take effect.
Practical checklist
  • Choose a global level that limits noise, usually INFO.
  • Enable DEBUG only for specific modules you need to inspect.
  • Collect logs to a centralized store before raising verbosity in production.
  • Revert verbose settings once you have the necessary data.
Common mistake
Leaving DEBUG on across all modules in production causes high log volume, storage strain, and possible performance impact.

screens.title: Understanding log levels
screens.narratorSegment: Log levels control message verbosity and are essential to balance information with cost. Fabric commonly uses CRITICAL, ERROR, WARNING, INFO, DEBUG, and sometimes FATAL. Use CRITICAL or FATAL only for unrecoverable conditions; these entries are rare but essential for alerts. ERROR should capture operational failures you must fix. WARNING surfaces potential issues that deserve attention but are not necessarily breaking. INFO is the standard operational level that provides a readable audit trail without excessive volume. DEBUG is very verbose and meant for development or targeted troubleshooting. A good practice is to run production at INFO and elevate individual modules to DEBUG only when investigating a problem. A misconception is thinking DEBUG equals more security; in fact it can reveal sensitive internal state and should be avoided unless logs are handled securely. Consider the example of troubleshooting gossip: set global INFO and gossip=DEBUG so you capture detailed peer discovery steps without exponentially increasing log throughput from unrelated modules. Closing thought: when you raise verbosity, ensure your log pipeline can handle the throughput and that retention policies meet compliance requirements. Understanding log levels means default to info in production; use targeted debug for short-lived troubleshooting to avoid overload and exposure.. In practical terms, which level to use and when. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Logging Levels
Level comparison
CRITICAL / FATAL
Only unrecoverable or system-fatal errors. Trigger alerts immediately.
ERROR
Operational failures you must fix; retain for diagnostics.
WARNING
Potential issues that deserve review but may not break flows.
INFO
Standard operational messages; preferred default for production.
DEBUG
Highly verbose, used for development or short, targeted troubleshooting of specific modules.
Practical rules
  • Run production at INFO by default to maintain readable audit trails.
  • Use module overrides like gossip=DEBUG only temporarily to collect specific diagnostics.
  • Monitor storage and pipeline throughput before enabling DEBUG across many components.
  • Avoid DEBUG in production where logs might reveal sensitive internal state.
Key Takeaway

Balance information and cost: prefer INFO, elevate modules selectively, and plan retention.

screens.title: What Fabric components log
screens.narratorSegment: Each Fabric component emits different log types and together they form a complete audit trail. Peers log transaction lifecycle events, chaincode execution prints, and gossip activity for state synchronization. Orderers log ordering decisions, block cut events, and delivery interactions. CAs log certificate issuance, revocation actions, and authentication events. Client applications usually add request-specific logs and often include transaction IDs. Chaincode prints appear inside peer logs under a chaincode module tag and are valuable when debugging business logic. A practical example: if a transaction is rejected due to endorsement policy, the endorsement phase logs on peers will include why an endorsement failed while the orderer will show if the transaction never reached the ordering service. A common mistake is ignoring MSP logs; identity verification problems often surface there, and missing them slows root cause analysis. For operations, collect logs from all these components, ensure consistent timestamps, and include metadata like host and component name so a central index can answer questions like which peer produced a specific chaincode print. What Fabric components log means peers, orderers, cas, chaincode and clients each provide pieces of the audit trail—collect them all and correlate.. In practical terms, peers, orderers, cas, chaincode and client applications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Component Logs
Component audit trails
  • Peers: Transaction lifecycles, endorsements, commits, gossip messages.
  • Orderers: Ordering, block creation, delivery operations.
  • CAs: Certificate issuance, revocation, and authentication events.
  • Chaincode: Business logic prints appearing under the chaincode module.
Example scenario
If an endorsement is rejected, peer endorsement logs will show validation errors; if a block is missing, orderer delivery logs will indicate if the transaction reached the ordering service.
Operational notes
  • Ensure logs include component and host metadata for accurate indexing.
  • Preserve chaincode prints by collecting peer stdout where chaincode container output is forwarded.
  • Maintain time synchronization across hosts so timestamps align during correlation.
Why it matters
Different components tell different parts of a story. Collect all parts to reconstruct full transaction events and identity validations.

screens.title: Analyzing transaction lifecycle logs
screens.narratorSegment: Tracing a transaction requires locating the lifecycle messages that appear across peers and orderers. The lifecycle begins when a proposal arrives at a peer. Look for endorsement module messages confirming signature validation and endorsement responses. Next, the client sends the endorsed proposal to the ordering service; orderer logs will show receipt and block assembly. Finally, peers receive the block and commit transactions, with committer logs showing validation and state updates. A concrete example is: invoke a simple asset creation chaincode, note the transaction ID printed by the client, then search peer logs for that ID. You should find the chaincode execution prints, endorsement responses, an ordering acknowledgement, and commit entries on committing peers. A common misconception is that a single log file contains everything; in distributed systems you must query multiple components and correlate by transaction ID and timestamp. When analyzing, ensure clocks are synchronized and consider adding application-specific correlation IDs to chaincode prints and client logs to speed cross-component searches. Closing question: what single identifier will you use to find the same transaction across peer and orderer logs? Analyzing transaction lifecycle logs means use transaction ids and synchronized timestamps to find matching entries across peers and orderers.. In practical terms, trace a transaction from proposal to commit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Transaction lifecycle
Numbered lifecycle steps
  1. 1. Proposal received — peer logs show proposal arrival and initial validation.
  2. 2. Endorsement — logs show endorsement results and any chaincode prints during execution.
  3. 3. Ordering — orderer logs show receipt and block cut events.
  4. 4. Delivery & commit — peer committer logs show validation and state updates.
Concrete example
Invoke a chaincode create asset, capture the transaction ID, then search logs for that ID in peer and orderer stores to follow the full path from proposal to commit.
Supporting hints
  • Ensure NTP or a time-sync service is configured across hosts for reliable timestamp correlation.
  • Use transaction IDs as the primary correlation key; add application IDs when helpful.
  • When possible, capture raw container stdout to preserve chaincode prints and module tags.
Key Takeaway

Follow transaction IDs across components and keep clocks in sync to build a reliable audit trail.

screens.title: Externalizing and centralizing Fabric logs
screens.narratorSegment: Externalizing logs means moving them out of ephemeral containers into a persistent, searchable system. When Fabric runs in Docker or Kubernetes, logs typically appear on stdout and are lost when containers are removed unless shipped. A reliable pipeline uses a log shipper on the host or as a sidecar—such as Filebeat or a Fluentd agent—to forward logs to a centralized store like Elasticsearch, Splunk, or Grafana Loki. The benefits are immediate: aggregated viewing across components, advanced search and filtering by transaction IDs, alerting on error patterns, and long-term retention for compliance. A practical approach is to tag each log entry with component and host metadata so queries can scope results quickly. Common pitfalls include failing to provision enough storage, ignoring retention policies, and not securing access to the central store. For an example, configure Filebeat to tail peer and orderer container logs and route them to Elasticsearch; then create a Kibana dashboard that highlights error rates and shows individual transaction traces. Ask yourself how you would set alerts to detect rising ERROR counts or unexpected authorization failures. Externalizing and centralizing Fabric logs means use agents or sidecars to forward container logs to a central store for search, alerting, and retention.. In practical terms, design a pipeline from container stdout to a persistent store. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: YAML configurations and their relationship to environment variables
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric components expose logging configuration in their YAML files, but environment variables like FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC provide a quick, runtime override. For peers, core. yaml includes logging sections that can set file destinations, formats, and levels. For orderers, orderer. yaml plays a similar role. The CA server uses its own YAML to control output behavior. However, FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC is commonly used to change verbosity without editing or redeploying configuration files. A practical workflow is to use FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC for short-term debugging and then, if a permanent change is required, update the appropriate YAML and perform a controlled rollout. Another operational consideration is where logs are written: YAML can be used to point logs to files instead of stdout, which is useful when a host-based collector expects files. A misconception is that changing the YAML always takes precedence; in many deployments the environment variable is evaluated at startup and can override or complement YAML values. When planning changes, document both temporary overrides and intended permanent settings so future operators understand why a level differs from the YAML baseline. screens.title: Chaincode output and correlation IDs
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode running inside the peer environment can emit prints or logs that appear in the peer's logfile under the chaincode module. These prints are invaluable for debugging business logic because they show runtime values and execution paths. A recommended practice is to include both the Fabric transaction ID and an application-specific correlation ID in chaincode prints. This lets you link chaincode behavior to client-side requests and to orderer or peer lifecycle messages. For example, when creating an asset, include the transaction ID and a short request ID in any print statements; then a single search in your central logging system will reveal the client submission, chaincode prints, endorsement logs, ordering acknowledgement, and commit entries. A common misconception is that chaincode prints are isolated; in reality they appear with module tags and timestamps and are searchable like any other log entry if you externalize them. Be careful about printing sensitive information. The closing exercise is to add a print to a simple chaincode, invoke it, and verify the print appears in the peer logs along with the transaction ID so you can trace the complete lifecycle.

How prints appear
Chaincode prints using the print function appear in the peer's logs tagged as chaincode module messages and include timestamps and transaction IDs where available.
Practical tip: add both Fabric transaction IDs and an application correlation ID to prints. This creates multiple ways to find the same execution across different log stores and components.
Example
Insert a print in chaincode that outputs the transaction ID and request ID, invoke the chaincode, and then search your centralized logs for that ID to see the full lifecycle.

screens.title: Best practices and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: There are a handful of repeatable practices that keep Fabric logging effective without introducing risk. First, default to INFO in production and use module-level DEBUG only temporarily. Leaving DEBUG enabled long-term can flood your storage and reveal internal state. Second, externalize logs off ephemeral containers to a central store to ensure durability and support retention policies required by auditors. Third, include metadata such as component name, host, and transaction ID so queries can be targeted and efficient. Fourth, create alerts for rising error rates or suspicious authorization failures so teams respond quickly. Common mistakes include not syncing clocks across hosts, which breaks time-based correlation, and failing to document temporary overrides, which causes confusion later. Another mistake is not provisioning enough index capacity in the central store, which leads to search failures during incidents. A concrete practice is to test an incident runbook: raise gossip verbosity for a suspected peer, collect logs to the central store, analyze the trace, then revert logging and archive the diagnostic set for audit. End with this question: what retention period will satisfy both operational debugging and compliance requirements in your context?

In Fabric, peers, orderers, certificate authorities, and client applications each emit logs that, when collected correctly, let you trace transactions, verify identity operations, and investigate incidents. This lesson will help you recognize the essential audit trails Fabric produces, configure logging verbosity safely, and move logs into a centralized system so they are durable and searchable. For example, you will learn how to set an environment variable to raise verbosity for the gossip protocol without flooding the entire network, how chaincode prints appear in peer logs, and why shipping container output to a central store matters for compliance. We'll also highlight common mistakes operators make, such as leaving debug-level logs on in production or failing to correlate transaction IDs across components. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to configure, interpret, and centralize Fabric logs to support troubleshooting, alerting, and audits. Consider what one successful transaction trace might reveal about peer health in your environment.

In this first set of objectives we focus on foundational understanding and configuration skills. You will first learn why comprehensive logging and auditing are essential: logs provide the evidence trail needed for compliance, forensic analysis, and operational debugging. A concrete example is extracting a transaction lifecycle from peer and orderer logs to reconstruct a disputed state change. Second, you'll learn how to configure logging levels for Fabric components using environment variables. Practically, this means editing container environment settings or process variables so FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC drives global and module-specific verbosity. We will show how an operator can raise gossip module verbosity without increasing noise from unrelated modules. Each objective pairs a skill with why it matters in production: better diagnostics, minimal performance impact, and audit readiness. As you study, consider how you would handle a live incident where a single peer reports timeouts. Which logs would you raise temporarily and how would you preserve them for later analysis?

This second objectives slide emphasizes operational application and diagnostic reasoning. You will practice editing Docker or container definitions to add FABRIC_LOGGING_SPEC and restart components to observe the effect. You will also learn to parse key audit trails: transaction lifecycle entries, chaincode prints, MSP logs, gossip, and channel configuration events. These are the events auditors and incident responders rely on. Finally, you will learn to design a central logging pipeline that preserves logs outside of ephemeral containers, supports search and alerts, and retains data for compliance. Think about how you would set alert thresholds for error rates and how correlation IDs improve traceability across peers and orderers.

Comprehensive logging and auditing mean you collect, preserve, and analyze records that prove what happened in your Fabric network and why. Logs are more than noise; they are the evidentiary trail auditors and incident responders use. For example, when a financial asset appears with an unexpected owner, transaction lifecycle logs from the peer and orderer can show when the proposal arrived, which endorsement results were returned, when ordering placed the transaction, and when peers committed the change. A common misconception is that local container logs are sufficient. One simple operational test is to deploy a chaincode with a print in its execution path and then perform an invoke; the chaincode print should appear in the peer's log with module tags that let you attach it to the transaction ID. Externalized logging refers to collecting container stdout and forwarding it to a centralized logging system; this prevents data loss when containers restart. An audit trail is the chronological record that ties events together across components; transaction lifecycle logs form the backbone of this trail.
